estimates.basis: Select Hugh Glasgow-1499 as the preferred possible father of James Glasgow-1509, the older Belfast/Larne ropemaker, at 52% subjective confidence, replacing William Glasgow-1505 in the local working tree. The archived chronology explicitly places a James, son of Hugh, at New Town/Larne in 1737 and identifies its reported 1762 Janet Shutter groom with that James. Hugh is an independently documented Larne merchant and elder, jointly leasing Newtown property in1736 and dealing with Hugh Shutter in the original1749 mortgage. The later James/Janet account and the distinctive Jane Shutter name in the younger William’s monument fit a recurring Glasgow–Shutter network. These combined named-parent, locality, generation and family-association clues favour Hugh over retaining a William father without a named-son record. This is a preferred working identification, not a proved father clause for the adult ropemaker. The chronology is one derivative reconstruction: its1737 child,1762 groom and reported1737–1802 stone must not be counted as three independent confirmations. The adult’s1737 birth may itself derive from that reconstruction; the independent1773 affidavit establishes only birth before27 October1743. The original1737 entry,1762 marriage and alleged James/Janet stone remain uninspected. Hugh Shutter’s relationship to Janet is unknown, and a business association does not identify a father-in-law. A different Hugh remains possible. No mother is selected: Ann is not established as the1737 child’s mother by the reviewed account. The monument’s separately recorded James Glasgow-3991, son of Hugh and Ann, died in1812 aged64 and belongs to the younger1747/48 generation. That is a serious rival explanation: the reported1737 child could have died and the name been used again. It is not a recorded death of that earlier child. Withdraw the categorical earlier inference that the1737 James must have died young. Do not equate the two James profiles, invent a second wife, or infer surviving brothers with the same forename as an established fact. The older ropemaker was already an adult in1760–1761 and over thirty in1773, so he remains distinct from the younger monument/tanner comparison.

estimates.basis: Select Hugh Glasgow-3956, the father named by Mary at her1862 marriage, as a probable brother of the1851 Glenleslie Robert represented within Glasgow-1367, at74% subjective confidence. Replace the existing uncertain father–son interpretation locally. The original1851 return expressly calls the unmarried34-year-old Antrim-born linen weaver Mary Glasgow Robert’s niece. The1862 Ballymena marriage expressly names the bride Mary Glasgow’s father as Hugh Glasgow,weaver. A same-surname niece whose father shares her weaving trade gives a coherent paternal-brother explanation; Hugh can belong to Robert’s generation without an invented intervening father. This promotes a long-recorded conditional inference into a selected working relationship, rather than discovering a new source or a new named relative. The74% is a combined judgment about identity and relationship, not a calculated frequency. Glasgow-1367 also carries unresolved Lisnagaver and other identity comparisons; the brother inference neither identifies those property holders nor validates all children attached to that composite account. Their shared residence supports their own sibling comparison; it does not independently prove Mary’s Glenleslie identity. No mother, new parent, shared anonymous parent, vital date, identity merge or live WikiTree field is added.

Select William Glasgow-3586, the weaver at Achenyeards named as Jean’s father in the 1 October 1732 Dundonald baptism, as William Glasgow-4101’s possible father at 52% subjective confidence. The specific existing local household offers a more useful working placement than leaving the 1733 child isolated: the children share the uncommon surname and parish, their entries occur on nearby pages of the same register, and the boy’s William name agrees with the proposed father. The existing father account is already paired with Barbara Stevenson, the boy’s named mother, but that tree pairing has not been traced to an independent marriage or full-parent entry and is not counted as additional proof. The whole father proposition remains an indirect household reconstruction.
estimates.limitations: The 1733 transcript has no father field or residence; absence from a transcript does not establish what the manuscript contains or prove illegitimacy. The 1732 transcript names William, weaver at Achenyeards, but no mother. Their baptisms are only 254 days apart, about eight and a half months: close spacing weakens a routine successive-infant-birth interpretation, while unknown birth dates and possible delayed baptism leave the proposed siblings compatible. Do not manufacture birth dates to resolve it. Another Glasgow father, a different Barbara Stevenson, and two separate local families remain alternatives. Barbara’s identification with her own 1733 citation is strong; the adult couple and cross-child father assignment are separate inferences. No mother is assigned to Jean, no full-sibling claim is made, and the existing ungraded Jean-to-William father relationship is unchanged. The earlier Ayrshire William accounts Glasgow-1055, Glasgow-3288 and Glasgow-1061 remain compatible wider comparisons; estimated ages or missing family details do not exclude them. No record links this father to any of their birth families, so no upstream father is selected. No later newspaper, maritime or American identity is inferred for the child. Exact percentages are individual judgments, not measured frequencies. Original register images were not newly inspected and no live WikiTree edit is made.

Select Isobell/Elizabeth Duffe (Duffe-18) as James Glasgow-4114’s probable working mother at 72% subjective confidence, through the preferred Edinburgh Duffe household. His marriages to Bessie Whyte on 6 July 1649 and Agnes Duncan on 11 November 1653, followed by Agnes’s burial as the weaver’s wife on 21 January 1674, permit a later Duffe household beginning in 1677. Select Robert Glasgow-1156 as James-2682’s probable working father at 61%, conditional on that preferred adult identity and the existing 86% identification of the 1641 apprentice’s named father Robert with the Duddingston account buried in 1647. estimates.scope: The main weaknesses are a very long working life and late fatherhood through 1691, together with the absence of a marriage, prior-wife clause, address, witness or admission-date reference directly joining the Duffe husband to the 1649 burgess. The cancelled 1690 Lindsayland apprenticeship could concern the 1696 son, but its deceased father would conflict with assigning that father to the living 1693 master; resolve this before a merge. Retain both James profiles as accounts of potentially one adult, not two proved sons of Robert. estimates.basis: Prefer the Irvine father account William Glasgow-1055 as the same adult as the Dundonald weaver William Glasgow-3586, at 56% subjective identity confidence. The Irvine entries name Wm or William as father of Grizell in 1724, Agnes in 1725, Katherine in 1727 and Margaret in 1729. The Dundonald entry names William Glasgow, weaver at Achenyeards, as Jean’s father on 1 October 1732. An existing adult household in the adjoining Irvine parish followed by the 1732 Dundonald household is a specific chronological and local fit, and is preferred to matching an otherwise untraced childhood profile alone. This is an inferred adult identity: the Irvine transcripts do not state the father’s trade or Achenyeards residence. Select John Glasgow-1057 as the Dundonald William’s possible working father at 46%. This is an assessment of the complete father proposition, including both the 56% adult identity and the further identification of the Irvine adult with the Stevenston child cited as born or baptised on 30 November 1700 to John Glasgow and Agnas Spark (OPR615,10/3,frame11). The current William-1055 account estimates 1701; the citation and estimate are not silently harmonised. John-1057 is the existing account for that named parent. Its separate identification with an Edinburgh child baptised in1661, and its own earlier ancestry, retain their existing qualifications. The percentages are individual judgments, not measured frequencies or independent values to multiply.
estimates.scope: No record names the Dundonald father’s own parents, connects the two adult households, or supplies an occupation for the Irvine father. William Glasgow-3288, baptised at Kilbirnie on20August1704, remains a compatible alternative. William Glasgow-1061, whose maintained transcript gives birth25June1715 and baptism26June1715 at Byres,Kilwinning, could have been a father at seventeen in1732; this is a weaker generation fit, not an exclusion. Katherine’s1727 transcript names Mary Monfodd, while the other three Irvine entries name Margaret with Monfood/Montford/Montfod variants; this maternal distinction remains unresolved. The undated Mary Montfort marriage attached to William-1061 cannot identify the1727 mother merely by her name. No maternity is transferred from either William account. The two William profiles remain separate accounts, with no merge and no claim of two proved William sons. Jean’s existing father link stays ungraded. The1733 child’s selected father remains possible52%, and Barbara Stevenson’s maternity remains99%; neither is strengthened by this upstream hypothesis. Jean’s mother remains unknown. Barbara’s existing pairing with the Dundonald father is ungraded and does not establish a remarriage after the Irvine household. Preserve all vital fields and previously selected relatives. Resolve the possible duplicate before a live attachment or merger. This is one new possible father proposal based on reassessment of held transcripts and profile citations; no original parish register was newly inspected and no live edit is made.

estimates.basis: Select the record-defined Lillias Stewart as the probable mother of James Glasgow-1483 at 86% subjective confidence. estimates.scope: The 86% assesses the complete maternity proposition for the adult James, including the child-to-adult identity. No birth, death, parents or childhood identity is assigned to Lillias from the contributed 1766 estimate.

estimates.basis: The 1786 Currituck Isaac account fits the exact seven-child family. The will independently names Isaac and the other six children; the later Tennessee identification is not proved by this will. The skeletal Glasgow-2363 account remains a possible duplicate. William Glasgow’s Currituck will, dated 14 October 1805 and recorded 22 January 1806, names wife Sarah, sons Caleb, Isaac, Samuel and John C., and daughters Ruth, Love Bright and Sophia. Its land divisions and household bequests identify one specific family. The named wife and all seven child names strongly identify the maintained William-357 family, with John C. compatible with John Cooper and Love now recorded under Bright; this conjunction outweighs the unsourced August death claim. The will also transfers an enslaved boy; that clause does not add a biological family relationship.

estimates.basis: Select Andrew Glasgow-1239 as the possible working father of Alexander Glasgow-3612. The inspected 17 April 1757 Mid Calder transcript names Alexander, father Andrew Glasgow and mother Janet Young. The adult Alexander’s uncertain 1760 birth and Newton/Midlothian family are compatible with this child: a 1757 child would be about 20 at his son George’s reported 1777 birth. The three-year difference from an uncertain birth field is not an exclusion. Andrew-1239’s 21 December 1729 Livingston baptism places a documented Andrew in the neighbouring parish and the right generation, aged about 27 in 1757. This is the preferred available regional and chronological reconstruction, rather than leaving the named-parent lead entirely outside the working tree.
estimates.scope: 42% is a subjective assessment of the complete adult Alexander → Andrew-1239 profile pair, including both the 1757 child-to-adult identification and the identification of the named Andrew with the Livingston child. Neither identity is proved by a shared occupation, witness, holding or later parent clause. The record-defined father’s given name and surname are explicit; that does not make this later profile pair confident. Andrew-3052, associated with Janet Clerk and an earlier Alexander household, remains an unselected possible alternative at 32%; a different spouse is not an exclusion. Other or unrepresented Andrews remain possible. No percentages are multiplied, and the two Andrew hypotheses are not independent propositions. Janet Young is the recorded mother but no modern mother identity is assigned. All vital fields, spouses and existing child links remain unchanged.

estimates.basis: Select James Glasgow-2492, the older Smith County householder, as Wesley Guynn Glasgow-2476’s possible working father. Their maintained accounts cite James in Smith County in 1820 and 1840 and the younger Wesley/Neely household there in 1850. James’s approximate 1776 birth makes him about 42 at Wesley’s estimated 1818 birth, a comfortable direct generation. The older James is a specific existing local household, not an invented parent. This is the leading bounded catalogue comparison for the disconnected Wesley family; its same-county chronology is more specific than an otherwise unplaced Tennessee or Scottish Glasgow.
estimates.scope: 35% is a subjective, low-confidence estimate for the complete father-profile hypothesis. No inspected record calls Wesley James’s son, places them in one household, transfers land between them, or names Wesley’s parents. The cited 1820/1840/1850 census images and age-band counts were not newly inspected; FamilySearch required a security challenge and the linked Ancestry record required membership. Wesley’s memorial has no parent links, dates or photograph beyond an approximate birth/death note; it is not independent parent proof. Wesley’s identification with the indexed Neely and James’s earlier North Carolina ancestry are separate propositions. An uncle or other collateral relationship, another local James, an unrepresented father, and William-2130 (broad Tennessee context without a held Smith County association) remain alternatives. No mother is selected and no relative is moved solely because of a name, naming custom or Y-DNA premise.
